grammarian-topic-nouns/grammarian-topic-:
A **noun** is a word that names something:
- a person (teacher)
- a place (kitchen)
- a thing (phone)
- an idea (luck).

Most nouns are **common nouns**. They name any member of a group, so they start with a small letter unless they begin a sentence: a city, the river, my brother.

A **proper noun** is the name of one particular person, place, day, month, company or event. It always starts with a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence: London, the Amazon, Friday, July, Toyota.

A quick test: if you can put "a" or "the" in front of it and it still means any one of many, it is common. If it is a name that points to one thing only, it is proper.

Singular means one; plural means more than one. Most nouns simply add **-s**: car, cars; idea, ideas. Nouns that end in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x or -z add **-es**, because the extra syllable makes them easier to say: glass, glasses; dish, dishes; watch, watches.

A consonant followed by -y changes to **-ies** (baby, babies), but a vowel followed by -y just adds -s (day, days; key, keys). Many nouns ending in -f or -fe change to **-ves**: knife, knives; leaf, leaves; half, halves.

A small group of common nouns are **irregular** and must be learned:
- man, men
- woman, women
- child, children
- person, people
- foot, feet
- tooth, teeth
- mouse, mice.

A few stay the same in both forms: sheep, fish, deer.

Nouns can also be grouped by what they name:
- **Concrete nouns** name things you can see, hear, touch, taste or smell: chair, music, rain, coffee.
- **Abstract nouns** name ideas, feelings and qualities you cannot touch: freedom, fear, honesty, advice.
- **Collective nouns** name a group as one unit: team, family, audience, staff, class.

In American English they usually take a singular verb (The team is ready); in British English a plural verb is also common when you think of the members (The team are arguing).

**Compound nouns** are made of two or more words working as one noun. They can be written as one word (toothbrush), as two words (bus stop) or with hyphens (mother-in-law).

Knowing the kind helps you choose articles and quantities: many abstract nouns are uncountable, so we say "some patience", not "a patience".

**Countable nouns** have a singular and a plural and can follow a number: one apple, three apples. **Uncountable nouns** have no plural and do not take a or an: water, rice, money, furniture, information, advice, homework.

Use many and a few with countable nouns (many questions, a few chairs), and much and a little with uncountable nouns (much time, a little sugar). A lot of and some work with both. In questions and negatives we usually use any: "Is there any milk?" "We don’t have any eggs."

To count an uncountable noun, put a **counting word** in front:
- a glass of water
- a piece of advice
- two pieces of information
- a bottle of oil.

Some nouns are both, with a change of meaning: "a coffee" (one cup) and "coffee" (the drink in general); "a light" (a lamp) and "light" (brightness).
grammarian-topic-pronouns/grammarian-top:
A **pronoun** takes the place of a noun so we do not repeat it: "Sara called. She was late."

**Subject pronouns** come before the verb and do the action: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. **Object pronouns** come after a verb or a preposition and receive the action: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. Compare "She helped us" with "We helped her".

A useful check in pairs: take the other person away. "Tom and me went home" sounds wrong once you remove Tom ("me went home"), so the correct form is "Tom and I went home". In the same way, "between you and me" is correct because between is a preposition and needs an object pronoun.

Use they for people in general, for a group, and for one person whose gender you do not know or who uses they.

Possessive words show who something belongs to. **Possessive adjectives** come before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. **Possessive pronouns** stand alone, with no noun after them: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. Compare "This is my bag" with "This bag is mine".

Notice that none of these words uses an apostrophe. It’s with an apostrophe always means it is or it has; its with no apostrophe shows possession: "The dog wagged its tail." In the same way, they’re means they are, there points to a place, and their shows possession.

For nouns, add **’s** to show possession (Ana’s phone, the teacher’s desk) and only an apostrophe after a plural -s (the students’ books).

**Reflexive pronouns** end in -self or -selves and refer back to the subject: "She taught herself Spanish." They are also used for emphasis: "I fixed it myself." Do not use them instead of a simple object: "Send it to me", not "to myself".

**Demonstrative pronouns** point: this and these for things near you, that and those for things further away. **Indefinite pronouns** refer to people or things in general: someone, anybody, everyone, nothing, each. They take a singular verb: "Everyone is here."

**Relative pronouns** (who, which, that, whose) join extra information to a noun: "the woman who called". **Interrogative pronouns** (who, what, which, whose) ask questions.

Each kind does a different job, but all of them save you from repeating a noun.
grammarian-topic-possessive-s-and-of/gra:
To show that something belongs to a person or an animal, add **’s** to the owner: Anna’s phone, the dog’s bed, my teacher’s car. The owner comes first and the thing comes second.

When the owner is a regular plural that already ends in -s, add **only the apostrophe**: my parents’ flat, the students’ results. Irregular plurals that do not end in -s add ’s as usual: the men’s room, people’s ideas.

A name that ends in -s can take ’s or just an apostrophe; both are accepted: Chris’s idea, Chris’ idea.

For things, places and parts of something, English usually uses **of** instead:
- the door of the car
- the end of the street
- the middle of the night
- the title of the book.

Many fixed time and place phrases still use **’s**: today’s news, the world’s population, a week’s holiday.

**Whose** asks about the owner: Whose jacket is this? Do not confuse it with who’s, which means who is.
grammarian-topic-articles-and-determiner:
**A** and **an** are indefinite articles. Use them with a singular countable noun when you mention something for the first time or mean any one: "I saw a fox." Choose by sound, not spelling: an before a vowel sound (an apple, an hour, an MP), a before a consonant sound (a book, a university, a one-way street).

**The** is the definite article. Use it when both people know which one you mean:
- because it was mentioned before ("The fox ran away")
- because there is only one (the sun, the internet)
- because the rest of the sentence makes it clear (the book on the table).

Use **no article** for plural or uncountable nouns in general statements: "Dogs need exercise." "Water boils at 100 degrees." Many fixed expressions also take no article: go to school, at home, by bus, have lunch.

A **determiner** comes before a noun and tells us which one or how much. Articles are determiners, and so are this/that/these/those, my/your/their, and quantity words.

**Quantifiers** depend on whether the noun is countable:
- With plural countable nouns use many, a few, few, several, a number of.
- With uncountable nouns use much, a little, little, a great deal of.
- Some, any, a lot of, plenty of, no and enough work with both.

**A few** and **a little** are positive (some, enough to be useful); few and little without a are negative (not enough): "I have a few friends here" sounds happy; "I have few friends here" sounds lonely.

Each and every take a singular noun (every student), while all and both take a plural (all students, both hands).
grammarian-topic-much-many-a-few-and-a-l:
**Countable nouns** have a plural (one chair, two chairs), so they go with many and a few. **Uncountable nouns** have no plural (water, money, advice, information, furniture), so they go with much and a little.

In questions we ask **How many…?** for things we count and **How much…?** for amounts.

In ordinary positive sentences, **a lot of** or lots of is more natural than much and works with both kinds: a lot of friends, a lot of time. Much is common in questions and negatives: Is there much traffic? We don’t have much time.

**A few** and **a little** are positive: they mean some, not many, but enough. **Few** and **little** without a are negative: they mean almost none, and often suggest a problem.

Compare:
- I have a few friends here, so I’m happy.
- I have few friends here, so I feel lonely.

Very few and very little make the negative meaning stronger. Quite a few means a fairly large number.
grammarian-topic-adjectives-and-comparis:
An **adjective** describes a noun or pronoun. It can come before the noun (a quiet street) or after a linking verb such as be, look, seem, feel, become (the street is quiet; you look tired).

English adjectives never change for plural or gender: a red car, two red cars. Do not add -s. Adjectives answer questions like what kind, which one, and how many: an old map, the last bus, three blue chairs.

Some adjectives come from nouns or verbs and have typical endings:
- -ful (helpful)
- -less (careless)
- -ous (famous)
- -able (comfortable)
- -al (natural)
- -ive (active)
- -y (sunny).

Recognising these endings helps you spot adjectives in a sentence and build your own.

When several adjectives come before a noun, native speakers follow a **usual order**: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose, then the noun. So we say "a lovely old Italian leather bag", not "an Italian old leather lovely bag". Two or three adjectives are plenty in most sentences.

Adjectives ending in -ed and -ing are easy to confuse. The **-ed** form describes how a person feels: bored, interested, tired, surprised. The **-ing** form describes the thing that causes the feeling: boring, interesting, tiring, surprising.

"I was bored because the film was boring." If you say "I am boring", you are saying that you make other people bored.

To compare two things, use a **comparative + than**. One-syllable adjectives add -er: tall, taller; cheap, cheaper. Double a final consonant after one short vowel (big, bigger) and change -y to -ier (easy, easier). Longer adjectives use more or less: more expensive, less comfortable.

To pick out one thing from a group of three or more, use the **superlative** with the: the tallest, the easiest, the most expensive.

Learn the irregular forms:
- good, better, the best
- bad, worse, the worst
- far, further, the furthest.

To say two things are equal, use **as + adjective + as**: "My phone is as old as yours." In the negative, not as … as means less: "It isn’t as cold as yesterday."
grammarian-topic-adverbs/grammarian-topi:
An **adverb** describes a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole sentence. It answers questions such as how, when, where, how often and how much.

Many adverbs of manner are formed by adding **-ly** to an adjective:
- quick, quickly
- careful, carefully
- happy, happily.

Some common adverbs look exactly like adjectives: fast, hard, late, early, straight. "She works hard" (not "hardly"). Be careful: hardly means almost not, and lately means recently. Good is an adjective; its adverb is **well**: "She is a good singer. She sings well."

Adverbs can also make adjectives stronger or weaker: very tired, quite good, extremely cold, a bit late.

**Adverbs of manner** (slowly, well) usually go after the verb or after the object: "She speaks English fluently", not "She speaks fluently English".

**Adverbs of frequency** (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never) go before the main verb but after be: "I often walk to work." "He is always late."

**Adverbs of time** (today, yesterday, soon, already) and place (here, outside, upstairs) usually go at the end, or at the start for emphasis: "Tomorrow we leave." When several come together at the end, the usual order is manner, place, time: "She sang beautifully at the concert last night."

**Sentence adverbs** such as unfortunately, honestly and clearly comment on the whole sentence and usually go first, followed by a comma.
grammarian-topic-conjunctions-and-interj:
Conjunctions are joining words. **Coordinating conjunctions** join words, phrases or whole sentences of equal weight. The seven are easy to remember as **FANBOYS**: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

And adds information, but shows contrast, or gives a choice, so shows a result, yet means but surprisingly, nor adds a second negative, and for (formal) means because.

When a coordinating conjunction joins two complete sentences, put a comma before it: "It was raining, so we stayed in." When it joins two short items, no comma is needed: "tea or coffee", "tired but happy".

**Subordinating conjunctions** introduce a clause that depends on another clause: because, although, when, while, if, unless, since, after, before, until. The clause they start cannot stand alone.

"Because I was tired" is not a full sentence; it needs a main clause: "I went to bed early because I was tired." If the dependent clause comes first, put a comma after it: "Although it was late, we kept talking."

**Interjections** are short words that show feeling or react quickly: oh, wow, oops, ouch, hey, well. They stand outside the grammar of the sentence and are followed by a comma or an exclamation mark: "Wow, that was fast!" They belong mostly in speech and informal writing.
grammarian-topic-sentence-building/gramm:
Every complete English sentence needs a **subject** and a **verb**. The subject is who or what the sentence is about; the verb says what the subject does or is. "Birds sing." "The meeting started." "I am hungry."

English almost always needs a stated subject, even when the meaning is obvious: say "It is raining" and "It is three o’clock", with the empty subject it, not just "Is raining".

The basic order is **subject – verb – the rest**. Questions and some special patterns change this order, but ordinary statements keep it. To find the subject, ask who or what before the verb: "Who started? The meeting."

Many verbs need an **object**: the person or thing that receives the action. The order is **subject – verb – object**: "Kim plays the piano." Do not put an adverb between the verb and its object: "I like coffee very much", not "I like very much coffee".

Some verbs take two objects, a person and a thing: give, send, show, tell, buy, lend. You can say "She gave me the key" or "She gave the key to me".

Linking verbs such as be, become, seem and feel are followed by a **complement**, not an object; it describes the subject: "She became a doctor." "He seems calm."

After the core, you can add place and time: "Kim plays the piano at school on Mondays."

A command (the **imperative**) uses the base form of the verb with no subject: "Sit down." "Turn left at the bank." "Be careful." For a negative command, add **don’t**: "Don’t touch that." "Don’t be late."

Commands can sound too direct in English, so we soften them in most situations. Add please, or turn the command into a question with can, could or would: "Could you close the window, please?" "Would you mind waiting here?" (Would you mind is followed by -ing.)

**Let’s + base verb** makes a suggestion that includes the speaker: "Let’s take a break." Commands are normal in instructions, recipes, signs and warnings, where short and clear is polite enough.
grammarian-topic-there-is-and-there-are/:
Use **there is** and **there are** to say that something exists or to mention it for the first time. There is goes with a singular noun or an uncountable noun; there are goes with a plural noun. In speech, there is is usually shortened to there’s.

Many languages use a verb like have for this idea, but English does not: say There is a museum in my town, not In my town have a museum.

After there is or there are we often add where the thing is: on the table, in the city, near the station.

For questions, put is or are first: **Is there…? Are there…?** Short answers repeat there with is, isn’t, are or aren’t, and a short yes answer is never contracted.

For negatives, use **there isn’t** or **there aren’t**, often with any, or use there is no / there are no. To count, ask How many… are there?

In the past, use **there was** and **there were**.
grammarian-topic-this-that-these-and-tho:
**This** and **these** point to things near the speaker; **that** and **those** point to things farther away. This and that are singular; these and those are plural.

They can come before a noun (this book, those trees) or stand alone (I like this. Are those yours?). Distance can be in space or in time: this week is now, that week was in the past.

We use **this is** to introduce people (This is my colleague, Dev) and to say who we are on the phone (Hello, this is Mia).

**That** can refer back to something just said: That’s a great idea. These days means nowadays; in those days means at a time in the past.
grammarian-topic-be-have-and-do/grammari:
**Be** is the most common verb in English, and it is irregular. In the present:
- I am
- you are
- he/she/it is
- we are
- they are.

In speech and informal writing we contract it: I’m, you’re, she’s, it’s, we’re, they’re. Use be for names, jobs, age, feelings, places and descriptions: "I’m Ana. I’m a nurse. I’m 30. I’m tired." Note that English uses be for age and for being hungry, cold or right: "I am 25", not "I have 25 years".

For the negative, add **not**: "She isn’t here." "I’m not ready." For questions, move be in front of the subject: "Are you ready?" "Is it far?" Short answers repeat be: "Yes, I am." "No, it isn’t."

**Have** shows possession, relationships, illnesses and many everyday actions. In the present it is have for I, you, we, they and **has** for he, she and it. "I have two sisters." "She has a cold." "We have lunch at one."

In British English you will also hear **have got** with the same meaning for possession: "I’ve got a car."

For questions and negatives with ordinary have, use do or does: "Do you have a pen?" "He doesn’t have time." With have got, use have itself: "Have you got a pen?" "He hasn’t got time." Do not mix the two patterns: "Do you have…?" or "Have you got…?", never "Do you have got…?"

Most verbs need a helper to make present simple questions. Use **do** with I, you, we, they and **does** with he, she, it. The order is **(question word) + do/does + subject + base verb**: "Do you like jazz?" "Where does she work?"

Because does already shows the third person, the main verb loses its -s: "Does he play?" not "Does he plays?" Be does not use do: "Are you happy?" not "Do you are happy?"

In questions about the subject itself, no do is needed: "Who lives here?" (the answer is the subject: "Maria lives here").

To make a present simple verb negative, put **don’t** (do not) or **doesn’t** (does not) before the base form. Use don’t with I, you, we, they and doesn’t with he, she, it: "I don’t eat meat." "She doesn’t drive."

As in questions, the main verb loses its -s after doesn’t: "He doesn’t work on Fridays", not "He doesn’t works". Do not use don’t with be or with modal verbs: say "I’m not tired" and "I can’t swim".

Do can also be the main verb, meaning perform an activity. Then you may see it twice: "I don’t do my homework at night." "What does she do?" (= What is her job?)
grammarian-topic-can-can-t-and-could/gra:
**Can** is a modal verb. It has the same form with every subject and is followed by the base verb, with no to and no -s: She can drive.

We use it:
- for ability (I can type fast)
- for permission (You can sit here)
- for possibility (It can be cold at night).

The negative is **cannot** or **can’t**. Questions put can before the subject, without do: Can you hear me? Short answers repeat can or can’t after the subject.

**Could** is the past of can for general ability: When I was young, I could run fast. Its negative, **couldn’t**, is common for something that was not possible on one occasion: I couldn’t open the jar.

Could is also a polite way to make a request (Could you help me?) or to ask for permission (Could I leave early?). It can also suggest a possibility: We could take the train.
grammarian-topic-present-simple-and-pres:
Use the **present simple**:
- for routines (I get up at seven)
- things that are generally true (She lives in Lyon)
- facts (The sun rises in the east).

With he, she and it, the verb adds **-s** or **-es**: works, watches, goes. Questions and negatives use **do** or **does** with the base verb: Do you drive? He doesn’t eat fish.

Frequency words such as always, usually, often, sometimes and never go before the main verb.

Use **am, is or are + -ing**:
- for an action happening at the moment of speaking (She’s on the phone; she’s talking to her boss)
- for a temporary situation around now (I’m reading a great novel this week).

Words such as now, at the moment, today and this week often go with it.

**State verbs** — know, like, love, want, need, believe, own, understand — describe states rather than actions, so they normally stay in the simple form: I want a coffee, not I am wanting a coffee.
grammarian-topic-past-simple-and-past-co:
Use the **past simple** for an action that started and finished in the past, often with a time phrase such as yesterday, last week, in 2015 or two days ago.

Regular verbs add **-ed** (walk, walked); many common verbs are irregular (go, went; see, saw; buy, bought). Questions and negatives use **did + base verb**: Did you call her? I didn’t see it.

A story is usually a chain of past simple verbs: I opened the door, looked around and switched on the light.

Use **was or were + -ing**:
- for an action that was in progress at a moment in the past (At nine o’clock I was watching the news)
- to set the background of a story (The sun was shining and the birds were singing).

When a short action interrupts a longer one, the longer action is continuous and the short one is simple, often joined by **when** or **while**: I was cooking when the phone rang.
grammarian-topic-talking-about-the-futur:
English has no single future tense. Use **going to**:
- for plans and intentions already decided (We’re going to get married in June)
- for predictions based on evidence you can see now (Look at that queue; we’re going to be late).

Use **will**:
- for decisions made at the moment of speaking (It’s cold. I’ll close the window)
- for offers and promises (I’ll help you)
- for predictions based on opinion (I think it will be a close game).

The negative of will is **won’t**.

The **present continuous** is common for fixed arrangements, usually with a time and other people involved: I’m meeting Rosa for lunch tomorrow.

The **present simple** is used for timetables and schedules: The concert starts at eight.

After time words such as when, after, before, as soon as and until, and after if, use a **present tense** even though the meaning is future: I’ll text you when I arrive.
grammarian-topic-used-to-and-would/gramm:
**Used to + base verb** describes habits and states in the past that are no longer true: I used to bite my nails. She used to have long hair. Questions and negatives use did and use to, without -d: Did you use to walk to school? I didn’t use to like olives.

**Would + base verb** can also describe repeated past actions, especially in stories and memories: Every Sunday my dad would make pancakes.

Would is not used for past states: say I used to own a motorbike, not I would own a motorbike.

**Be used to** means something is familiar and no longer strange; it is followed by a noun or an -ing form: I’m used to the noise. She’s used to working long hours.

**Get used to** describes the process of becoming familiar: It took me months to get used to driving on the left.

Do not mix them up with used to + base verb, which is only about the past.
grammarian-topic-verbs/grammarian-topic-:
**Action verbs** describe something someone does: run, write, decide. **Linking verbs** connect the subject to a description: be, seem, become, look, feel, sound.

**Auxiliary** (helping) verbs work with a main verb to make tenses, questions and negatives: be, have, do. **Modal verbs** (can, could, will, would, should, must, may, might) add meaning such as ability, possibility or obligation and are followed by the base form.

Verbs are also **transitive or intransitive**. A transitive verb needs an object: "She bought a ticket." An intransitive verb does not: "The baby slept." Many verbs can be both: "He opened the door" / "The door opened."

Finally, **state verbs** describe situations rather than actions (know, like, believe, own, need) and are rarely used in continuous tenses: "I know", not "I am knowing".

**Regular verbs** form the past simple and past participle with -ed: work, worked, worked; play, played, played. Spelling changes:
- add only -d after -e (live, lived)
- change consonant + y to -ied (study, studied)
- double a final consonant after one stressed short vowel (stop, stopped; plan, planned).

The -ed ending has three sounds:
- /t/ after voiceless sounds (walked)
- /d/ after voiced sounds (played)
- /ɪd/ after t or d (wanted, needed).

**Irregular verbs** have their own forms and must be learned:
- go, went, gone
- take, took, taken
- buy, bought, bought
- put, put, put.

The most common verbs in English are mostly irregular, so learning the top forty gives you most everyday sentences.

A **phrasal verb** is a verb plus one or two small words (particles) such as up, out, off, on, down, away: give up, find out, look after, run out of. The meaning is often different from the separate words, so learn each as a whole item: give up = stop trying; look after = take care of.

Some phrasal verbs are **separable**: the object can go in the middle or after the particle: "Turn off the light" or "Turn the light off". But a pronoun object must go in the middle: "Turn it off", never "Turn off it".

Others are **inseparable**; the object always follows: "She looks after her grandmother." "I ran into an old friend." A good dictionary shows which type a verb is, often with sb/sth in the position where the object goes.

When one verb follows another, the second verb is either a **gerund (-ing)** or an **infinitive (to + base form)**. The first verb decides.

Verbs such as enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, keep and consider take -ing: "I enjoy cooking." Verbs such as want, decide, hope, plan, agree, promise, refuse and need take to: "We decided to leave." After a preposition, always use -ing: "She is good at drawing." "Thanks for coming."

A few verbs take both with a **change of meaning**. "I stopped smoking" means I no longer smoke; "I stopped to smoke" means I stopped in order to smoke. "Remember to lock the door" is about the future; "I remember locking the door" is about a memory.
grammarian-topic-gerunds-and-infinitives:
When one verb follows another, the second verb is either an **-ing form** (a gerund) or **to + base verb** (an infinitive), depending on the first verb.

Verbs often followed by -ing include enjoy, finish, mind, avoid, suggest, keep, practise and consider: I don’t mind waiting.

Verbs often followed by to + verb include want, need, decide, hope, plan, promise, agree, refuse, learn and would like: She refused to pay. There is no rule that predicts every verb, so learn them in short phrases.

An **-ing form** can be the subject of a sentence (Running clears my head) and is always used after a preposition (She’s interested in learning Korean).

A few verbs take both forms with a **change of meaning**:
- Stop doing means end the activity; stop to do means pause in order to do it.
- Remember to do and forget to do look forward to a task; remember doing looks back at something you did.
- Try doing means experiment; try to do means make an effort.
grammarian-topic-phrasal-verbs/grammaria:
A **phrasal verb** is a verb plus a small word such as up, down, out, off, on, in or over. Together they make a new meaning that is often hard to guess from the parts:
- give up means stop
- look after means take care of
- find out means discover.

Phrasal verbs are very common in everyday speech, while a single formal verb is often used in writing:
- find out / discover
- put off / postpone
- call off / cancel.

Many phrasal verbs are **separable**: a noun object can go before or after the small word (Turn the lights off / Turn off the lights). But a pronoun object such as it, them or her must go in the middle: Turn them off, not Turn off them.

Some phrasal verbs **cannot be separated** (look after the baby, look after her), and some take **no object** at all (The plane took off).
grammarian-topic-so-such-too-and-enough/:
**So** and **such** make a quality stronger. So goes before an adjective or adverb on its own: so tired, so quickly.

Such goes before a noun phrase:
- such a long day (singular)
- such long days (plural)
- such good advice (uncountable).

Both can be followed by **that + a result**: The soup was so salty that nobody finished it. It was such a funny film that we watched it twice.

**Too** means more than is acceptable, and it goes before an adjective or adverb: too hot, too slowly. Too much and too many go before nouns.

**Enough** means as much as is needed; it goes after an adjective or adverb (warm enough, fast enough) but before a noun (enough money).

Both often continue with to + verb or for + person: This bag is too heavy for me. She’s old enough to vote.
grammarian-topic-prepositions/grammarian:
Prepositions show how things relate in time and space.

For time:
- use **at** for exact times and short moments (at 6 pm, at noon, at the weekend in British English)
- **on** for days and dates (on Monday, on 3 May, on my birthday)
- **in** for longer periods (in July, in 2026, in the summer, in the morning).

For place:
- use at for a point or a building as a place of activity (at the bus stop, at work, at the cinema)
- on for a surface or a line (on the table, on the wall, on the second floor, on Main Street)
- in for an enclosed space or area (in the box, in the car, in Spain).

Other useful prepositions: under, next to, between, opposite, behind, in front of, above, below. Learn fixed phrases as wholes: on the bus, in a taxi, at home, in bed, on time (punctual) and in time (early enough).

Some prepositions show **movement** towards or through something: to (a destination), into (entering a space), onto (moving to a surface), out of, across, through, along, past, towards. Compare "She walked in the park" (her position) with "She walked into the park" (entering it).

Arrive takes **at** for a building or point and **in** for a city or country: "We arrived at the hotel / in Rome", never "arrived to".

Many adjectives, verbs and nouns are followed by a **fixed preposition** that must be learned with the word: good at, afraid of, interested in, depend on, listen to, wait for, a reason for, an increase in. When you learn a new word, learn its preposition too, and write the whole phrase in your notes.
grammarian-topic-prepositions-after-word:
Many verbs are followed by a particular preposition, and the choice is not always logical, so it is best to **learn the pair**: listen to, wait for, depend on, belong to, apologise for, agree with someone, think about, look at, pay for.

When the preposition is followed by a verb, use the **-ing form**: She apologised for keeping us waiting. In questions the preposition often moves to the end: What are you looking at?

**Adjectives** also have fixed partners: good at, bad at, interested in, afraid of, proud of, tired of, keen on, responsible for, similar to, different from, married to. Some **nouns** do too: a reason for, an increase in, a difference between, an answer to, advice on.

Using the wrong preposition rarely stops people understanding you, but it is one of the clearest signs of a learner.
grammarian-topic-questions/grammarian-to:
**Yes/no questions** put an auxiliary or be in front of the subject: "Are you ready?" "Can she swim?" "Did they call?" **Wh- questions** start with a question word and then follow the same order: **question word + auxiliary + subject + main verb**. "Where do you live?" "Why did he leave?" "How long have you been here?"

Choose the question word for the information you want:
- who (person)
- what (thing)
- where (place)
- when (time)
- why (reason)
- which (choice from a set)
- whose (owner)
- how (way)
- how much/many (amount).

When the question word is the subject, there is no auxiliary: "Who called you?" (someone called), but "Who did you call?" (you called someone). **Indirect questions** are more polite and use statement order: "Could you tell me where the station is?", not "where is the station".

A **question tag** is a short question added to the end of a statement, used to check information or invite agreement: "You’re coming, aren’t you?" Use the same auxiliary as the statement, or do/does/did if there is none.

A positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag: "She lives here, doesn’t she?" "They didn’t call, did they?" The tag after I am is aren’t I. Falling intonation on the tag means you expect agreement; rising intonation means it is a real question.

**Short answers** repeat the auxiliary rather than the whole verb: "Do you like it?" "Yes, I do." "Can she drive?" "No, she can’t." They sound more natural than just yes or no.
